It asks for very little in the way of cost or preparation.

Walks among greenery eased tiredness more than roadside walks.

Their purchases were larger but their visits less frequent.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main point in the final paragraph?

Fairly cheap adjustments can greatly change how a place feels.
Grand plans are needed before individuals start walking more.
Older people gain most from improvements to street design.

blocks.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

people.name: Wanjiru Delgado
people.role: psychologist who studied the effect of lunchtime walks on office workers

people.name: Matthias Okeke
people.role: transport planner who studied shoppers' spending before and after a high street was closed to cars

paragraphs.text: For almost all of human history, getting from one place to another meant putting one foot in front of the other. Walking was not a hobby or a fitness plan; it was simply how life worked. Today, in many wealthy countries, even journeys of less than two kilometres are routinely made by car, and the humble act of walking has come to seem slightly old-fashioned. Yet a growing number of doctors, planners and ordinary citizens are rediscovering what our ancestors took for granted: that travelling on foot may be one of the cheapest and most effective ways to improve both our own lives and the places we live in.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The physical benefits are well established. Researchers have found that regular brisk walking reduces the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and several other serious conditions, and it helps people keep a healthy weight as they age. Health authorities commonly advise adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, and a brisk half-hour walk on five days meets that target. What makes walking so attractive is how little it demands. There is no membership fee, no special kit beyond a decent pair of shoes, and no need to book a court or join a team. It is also gentle on the joints, so people who have never thought of themselves as sporty can start without much fear of injury.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The rewards are not only physical. Many people say a walk helps them think more clearly, and there is evidence to support the feeling. In one study, the psychologist Wanjiru Delgado asked 120 office employees to take a twenty-minute walk during their lunch break for six weeks. Half walked through a nearby park, while the others followed a route along a busy main road. Both groups reported feeling less tired in the afternoons than before, but the improvement was noticeably greater among those who had walked among trees and grass. Delgado is careful not to overstate her results: the group was small, and the workers described their own moods rather than being measured by any test. Still, she believes the findings are worth taking seriously.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Walking also changes how people relate to one another. A driver passes through a neighbourhood behind glass; a pedestrian is part of it. People on foot nod to neighbours, stop to chat outside the bakery and notice when an elderly resident has not been seen for a few days. Urban thinkers have long argued that streets full of walkers feel safer, because so many people are quietly keeping an eye on what is going on. In areas where nearly every trip is made by car, by contrast, residents may live side by side for years without ever learning each other's names.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: There is an economic side to the story too. When councils propose removing traffic from shopping streets, local traders often protest, convinced that customers who cannot park outside will simply go elsewhere. The transport planner Matthias Okeke decided to test this fear. He surveyed shoppers on a high street in a medium-sized town before and after it was closed to cars. He found that people arriving on foot tended to spend less on each visit than drivers did, but they came back far more often, so that over a month they spent more in total. Okeke admits that one town cannot speak for every high street, but he considers the pattern hard to ignore. Several shops that had opposed the scheme later asked for it to be extended to neighbouring streets.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: If walking brings so many benefits, why do so many people avoid it? The usual explanation is laziness, but that is unfair. In much of the modern world, the environment itself discourages walking. Suburbs are often spread out, so that the nearest shop may be a long way from home. Pavements suddenly come to an end, wide roads are difficult and frightening to cross, and pedestrians may wait two minutes at a crossing for a green light that lasts only a few seconds. Even keen walkers give up when a ten-minute stroll means crossing a car park and a six-lane road. Faced with such conditions, choosing the car is a perfectly rational decision.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The encouraging news is that walking does not require expensive projects to flourish. Some of the most effective improvements are surprisingly modest: shortening the distance across busy junctions, giving pedestrians more time at traffic lights, planting trees that offer shade in summer, adding benches so that older people can rest, and improving street lighting so that evening walks feel safe. None of these measures costs as much as a new road, yet together they can transform how a place feels. Cities need not wait for grand plans, and nor do individuals. The next time a journey is short enough, leave the keys at home and see what you notice along the way.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
The Quiet Power of Walking

A. For almost all of human history, getting from one place to another meant putting one foot in front of the other. Walking was not a hobby or a fitness plan; it was simply how life worked. Today, in many wealthy countries, even journeys of less than two kilometres are routinely made by car, and the humble act of walking has come to seem slightly old-fashioned. Yet a growing number of doctors, planners and ordinary citizens are rediscovering what our ancestors took for granted: that travelling on foot may be one of the cheapest and most effective ways to improve both our own lives and the places we live in.

B. The physical benefits are well established. Researchers have found that regular brisk walking reduces the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and several other serious conditions, and it helps people keep a healthy weight as they age. Health authorities commonly advise adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, and a brisk half-hour walk on five days meets that target. What makes walking so attractive is how little it demands. There is no membership fee, no special kit beyond a decent pair of shoes, and no need to book a court or join a team. It is also gentle on the joints, so people who have never thought of themselves as sporty can start without much fear of injury.

C. The rewards are not only physical. Many people say a walk helps them think more clearly, and there is evidence to support the feeling. In one study, the psychologist Wanjiru Delgado asked 120 office employees to take a twenty-minute walk during their lunch break for six weeks. Half walked through a nearby park, while the others followed a route along a busy main road. Both groups reported feeling less tired in the afternoons than before, but the improvement was noticeably greater among those who had walked among trees and grass. Delgado is careful not to overstate her results: the group was small, and the workers described their own moods rather than being measured by any test. Still, she believes the findings are worth taking seriously.

D. Walking also changes how people relate to one another. A driver passes through a neighbourhood behind glass; a pedestrian is part of it. People on foot nod to neighbours, stop to chat outside the bakery and notice when an elderly resident has not been seen for a few days. Urban thinkers have long argued that streets full of walkers feel safer, because so many people are quietly keeping an eye on what is going on. In areas where nearly every trip is made by car, by contrast, residents may live side by side for years without ever learning each other's names.

E. There is an economic side to the story too. When councils propose removing traffic from shopping streets, local traders often protest, convinced that customers who cannot park outside will simply go elsewhere. The transport planner Matthias Okeke decided to test this fear. He surveyed shoppers on a high street in a medium-sized town before and after it was closed to cars. He found that people arriving on foot tended to spend less on each visit than drivers did, but they came back far more often, so that over a month they spent more in total. Okeke admits that one town cannot speak for every high street, but he considers the pattern hard to ignore. Several shops that had opposed the scheme later asked for it to be extended to neighbouring streets.

F. If walking brings so many benefits, why do so many people avoid it? The usual explanation is laziness, but that is unfair. In much of the modern world, the environment itself discourages walking. Suburbs are often spread out, so that the nearest shop may be a long way from home. Pavements suddenly come to an end, wide roads are difficult and frightening to cross, and pedestrians may wait two minutes at a crossing for a green light that lasts only a few seconds. Even keen walkers give up when a ten-minute stroll means crossing a car park and a six-lane road. Faced with such conditions, choosing the car is a perfectly rational decision.

G. The encouraging news is that walking does not require expensive projects to flourish. Some of the most effective improvements are surprisingly modest: shortening the distance across busy junctions, giving pedestrians more time at traffic lights, planting trees that offer shade in summer, adding benches so that older people can rest, and improving street lighting so that evening walks feel safe. None of these measures costs as much as a new road, yet together they can transform how a place feels. Cities need not wait for grand plans, and nor do individuals. The next time a journey is short enough, leave the keys at home and see what you notice along the way.

explanation.uk: В абзаці C обидві групи стали менше втомлюватися, але в групи, що гуляла в парку, покращення було помітнішим. Тож неправильно, що користь отримала лише група з парку. Жодних тестів не проводили: працівники самі описували свій настрій.

options.text: Their single visits were worth more than those of drivers.
Their frequent visits outweighed their smaller purchases.
Their numbers rose mainly in the streets near the scheme.
Their purchases were larger but their visits less frequent.

questions.prompt: What did Matthias Okeke find about shoppers who arrived on foot?
questions.evidence: they came back far more often, so that over a month they spent more in total

explanation.en: Paragraph E says walkers spent less on each visit than drivers but came back much more often, so they spent more over a month. Neighbouring streets are mentioned only because shops later asked for the scheme to be extended.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что пешеходы тратили за одно посещение меньше, чем водители, но приходили гораздо чаще, поэтому за месяц тратили больше. Соседние улицы упоминаются лишь потому, что позже магазины попросили распространить проект и на них.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що пішоходи витрачали за один візит менше, ніж водії, але приходили набагато частіше, тож за місяць витрачали більше. Сусідні вулиці згадано лише тому, що згодом крамниці попросили поширити проєкт і на них.

questions.prompt: The writer believes it is unfair to explain people's reluctance to walk as simply a matter of ______.
questions.evidence: The usual explanation is laziness, but that is unfair.

explanation.en: Paragraph F says the common explanation for not walking is laziness, but the writer calls this unfair and blames the design of places instead.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F сказано, что нежелание ходить пешком обычно объясняют ленью, но автор считает это несправедливым и винит в этом то, как спланированы места.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F сказано, що небажання ходити пішки зазвичай пояснюють лінощами, але автор вважає це несправедливим і вбачає причину в тому, як сплановано місця.

questions.prompt: Because many suburbs are ______, a shop can be a considerable distance from people's homes.
questions.evidence: Suburbs are often spread out, so that the nearest shop may be a long way from home.

explanation.en: Paragraph F explains that suburbs are often spread out, which is why the nearest shop may be far from home.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F объясняется, что пригороды часто сильно разбросаны, поэтому ближайший магазин может находиться далеко от дома.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F пояснюється, що передмістя часто дуже розкидані, тому найближча крамниця може бути далеко від дому.

questions.prompt: At some crossings, pedestrians wait a long time for a ______ that disappears after only a few seconds.
questions.evidence: wait two minutes at a crossing for a green light that lasts only a few seconds

explanation.en: Paragraph F says people may wait two minutes at a crossing for a green light that lasts only a few seconds.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F сказано, что на переходе людям порой приходится две минуты ждать зелёного сигнала, который горит всего несколько секунд.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F сказано, що на переході людям часом доводиться дві хвилини чекати зеленого сигналу, який горить лише кілька секунд.
